## Video transcript

This video explains how MSMS computes molecular surfaces.

Biological molecules exist in solvent, which is mostly water.

For the calculation, this water molecule is represented by a sphere. It rolls over the atoms of
the molecule to define the solvent excluded surface, or molecular surface for short.

MSMS first places the water molecule, here the large orange sphere, in a position where it
contacts three atomic spheres. This position defines a spherical triangle on the probe, shown as
an orange mesh, outlining the solvent excluded surface. It also corresponds to a vertex of the
solvent accessible surface, the center of the probe sphere, and to a triangular face of the
reduced surface, shown as a red triangle.

From such a position, the probe can roll over a pair of atoms until it hits a third atom. As it
rolls, it sweeps out a green toroidal face of the solvent excluded surface, while its center
travels along an edge of the solvent accessible surface, which corresponds to an edge of the
reduced surface.

This image gives an overview of the duality between the three surfaces: the reduced surface at
the bottom, the solvent excluded surface in the middle, and the solvent accessible surface at the
top. Knowing one of these surfaces defines the other two.

Here is MSMS at work on a small molecule. The probe rolls over the atoms, laying down gold
reentrant faces and green toroidal faces.

Once all reentrant faces have been defined, the open patches on the atomic spheres define contact
faces, shown in purple.

Triangles for these faces are obtained by clipping a pre-triangulated template with the face
outline, and stitching them to the edges of the green toroidal faces.

The mathematical definition of these surfaces, and the MSMS software to compute them, were
published thirty years ago, in 1996. MSMS is still widely used today.
:::

In 1996, Michel Sanner published *Reduced surface: an efficient way to compute molecular
surfaces* in *Biopolymers*, introducing MSMS, a program for
computing molecular surfaces efficiently and reliably.

Originally developed as part of Michel Sanner's PhD research, MSMS addressed an important
challenge in structural biology: generating accurate representations of the surfaces of proteins
and other molecules. These surfaces help researchers visualize molecular shapes and investigate
how molecules interact.

Over the following three decades, MSMS became a widely used tool in molecular modeling and
visualization, finding its way into applications such as VMD, UCSF Chimera, and PMV. The 1996
paper has been cited more than 2,700 times (2,721 according to Google Scholar on November 10,
2026).

What is particularly rewarding is that MSMS continues to find applications in new areas of
research. For example, a [2026 study of protein–membrane interactions](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.5c02566)
used MSMS to generate molecular surfaces for geometric deep-learning models. A tool originally
developed for molecular graphics is now contributing to research approaches that were difficult
to imagine in 1996.

Scientific software evolves rapidly, and many excellent tools have emerged since MSMS was
introduced. Seeing MSMS remain useful after 30 years is a gratifying reminder that a well-defined
computational solution can continue to serve the research community long after its original
development.

We are proud to mark this anniversary and grateful to the many researchers who have used, cited,
and built upon MSMS over the years.
